t: Contain Virus — Daily Simulation of Regions, Threats, and Walls
o: Each 'day' we must: (1) find every connected infected region via 4-directional connectivity; (2) for each region compute the set of uninfected cells it would infect tonight and how many walls quarantining it requires (one wall per boundary edge between the region and each threatened cell); (3) build walls around the region threatening the most new cells, adding its wall count to the answer; (4) let every other region spread into its threatened cells simultaneously. In Example 1, the left region threatens 5 cells needing 5 walls, is walled first; then the right region spreads and later needs 5 more walls. In Example 2, the ring region threatens only the center cell but touches it from 4 sides, so 4 walls are built. With m,n ≤ 50 there are at most ~2500 cells, so re-scanning the whole grid every day is easily fast enough.
k: Walls needed to quarantine a region = number of distinct boundary edges between region cells and threatened uninfected cells (a cell threatened by k sides costs k walls).
Only ONE region is walled per day; all other regions spread simultaneously, so analyze all regions before mutating the grid.
A fully walled region never changes again, so the process terminates in at most O(m·n) days.

a.n: Approach 1: Straightforward Daily Simulation with DFS
a.i: Every day, flood-fill each unvisited infected region. While filling, collect the set of adjacent uninfected cells (threats) and count boundary edges to them (walls). Pick the region maximizing threat count, add its wall count to the answer, mark its cells as permanently contained (e.g., set to -1), then spread every other region into its threatened cells. Repeat until no region can spread.
s: Scan the grid; for each unvisited infected cell, DFS to gather region cells, threatened neighbor set, and wall-edge count.
If no threats exist anywhere, stop and return the accumulated wall count.
Choose the region with the largest threat-set size; add its wall count to the answer and mark its cells as contained (-1).
For every other region, set each threatened cell to 1 (simultaneous spread).
a.t: O(D · m · n) where D ≤ m·n is the number of days; each day is a full grid scan with DFS, so worst case O((m·n)²) ≈ 6.25M operations for 50×50 — fast enough.
a.sp: O(m · n) for the visited matrix, stacks, and per-day region/threat storage.

a.n: Approach 2: Same Simulation with Region IDs and Edge Counting via Neighbor Sets
a.i: Identical high-level loop, but instead of counting wall edges during DFS, assign each region an ID and record, for each threatened cell, which region IDs border it. Walls for a region equal the total number of incident boundary edges, computed as sum over threatened neighbors of how many of their infected neighbors belong to that region. This variant makes the 'k sides ⇒ k walls' rule explicit and avoids any ambiguity about shared threatened cells between regions.
s: Label each region with a unique ID using DFS/BFS; store cells per ID.
For each uninfected cell adjacent to infection, record the multiset of neighboring region IDs.
Region threat size = number of distinct threatened cells; wall cost = total ID occurrences across those cells.
Wall the max-threat region (mark contained), then flip all other regions' threatened cells to infected.
a.t: Same asymptotics as Approach 1: O(D · m · n) per-day work with small constant-factor overhead from maps/sets; D ≤ m·n days.
a.sp: O(m · n) for region labels, threat maps, and per-day structures.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1: it directly mirrors the problem statement and is easy to verify. Key pitfalls: (1) walls count boundary *edges*, not threatened cells — Example 2 shows one threatened cell costing 4 walls; (2) all non-quarantined regions spread *simultaneously*, so compute all threats before mutating the grid; (3) use a sentinel like -1 for contained cells so they are neither infected nor spreadable; (4) remember a region with zero threats still blocks termination checks — stop when no region has threats. Edge cases: single-cell grid, already-disconnected regions, regions that merge after spreading (handled naturally since we relabel each day). Follow-ups: what if ties were allowed/broken differently, or if you could wall multiple regions per day (greedy choice may no longer be optimal); complexity could be improved with incremental region tracking, but at these constraints it is unnecessary.
